story: According to Dreamtime stories, the Wandjina were cloud and rain spirits who created the landscape and all its inhabitants, and who continued to hold influence over both. When each spirit found the place where it would die, it painted its own image on a cave wall and then entered a nearby waterhole. Aboriginal people later refreshed these paintings as a way of regenerating the life force of the spirits. The Wandjina were said to punish those who broke the law by sending floods, lightning, and cyclones. A closely related creator being called Wunggurr was described as a more diffuse life force underlying all things, comparable to the Rainbow Serpent found in other Aboriginal belief systems; one aspect of this being was embodied in a rock python known as Wanjad. In rock art, the Wandjina were painted in black, red, and yellow on a white background, shown alone or in groups, sometimes alongside figures such as the Rainbow Serpent or yams. They were typically depicted with large upper bodies and heads showing eyes and a nose but no mouth, because they were said to be so powerful they did not need speech, and because if they had mouths the rain would never cease. Around their heads, lines or blocks of color represented lightning emerging from transparent helmets. Each painting and site had its own name, and communities repainted the images, especially in December or January, to ensure both the continued presence of the spirits and the arrival of the monsoon rains.
